study.title: Jeremiah 11 The broken covenant and opposition to the prophet
study.overview: Jeremiah 11 presents the Lord reminding Judah of the covenant established with Israel since the exodus: hearing the voice of God was not optional, but the condition of the covenant relationship. The chapter shows that persistent disobedience was not an occasional slip, but a continuous and collective refusal to listen, follow and remain in the Lord's way. In view of this, the denunciation of infidelity, the announcement of unavoidable judgment, the prohibition of intercession in favor of the people at that time and, finally, the revelation of a conspiracy against Jeremiah in Anatothe, which leads to a specific sentence on his opponents.

outline.title: The memory of the covenant and its demands
outline.explanation: The Lord sends Jeremiah to proclaim the words of the covenant in Judah and Jerusalem. The remembrance of the exodus and the promise of the earth shows that the relationship with God was founded in redemption and obedience. The people would be of God, and God would be of the people, as long as they heard and practice their voice.

outline.title: The old refusal and the breaking of the covenant
outline.explanation: Jeremiah must repeat the appeal in the cities and streets, but the historical response of Israel was the same: not to hear, not to incline the ear and follow the hardness of one's own heart. The chapter treats this persistence as a violation of the covenant, a kind of community treason, which includes Judah and also the home of Israel.

outline.title: Judgment without escape and empty cult
outline.explanation: The consequence is calamity from which there will be no deliverance through other gods or through intercession at that time. The Lord rejects a cult marked by infidelity, describes Judah as a beautiful olive tree now destined for fire and shows that judgment itself comes because of idolatrous practices and provocation against him.

outline.title: The conspiracy against Jeremiah and the divine response
outline.explanation: Jeremiah receives knowledge of the plot armed by the men of Anathoth, who wish to silence him. The prophet hand over the cause to the Lord, the righteous judge, and God announces concrete punishment to the conspirators, including death and absence of survivors, at the appointed time of their visitation.

study.context: The given notes place the chapter in a period of Jeremiah's ministry in which Judah was still standing, but spiritually in crisis. Tyndale notes that the message was addressed to the men of Judah and Jerusalem in legal language of accusation. Adam Clarke suggests that the speech would have been delivered in the first year of Zedekiah, but this appears as an interpretative hypothesis, not as a certain data of the text. The immediate scenario is that of a community that preserved religious forms, but had broken the fidelity demanded by the covenant.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes that the Lord's covenant is not mere national privilege, but moral and spiritual commitment. Listening to the voice of God means obeying in a concrete way; continuous disobedience reveals a rebellious heart, not just an external failure. The text also teaches that worship can become empty when separated from fidelity: sacrifices, incense and religious invocation do not replace obedience. There is also a dimension of divine justice: the Lord sees betrayal, judges collective sin and does not let himself be manipulated by rites or cries made without repentance. Finally, Jeremiah appears as a figure of the faithful servant who suffers opposition even among his own, entrusting his cause to the righteous judge.

scholarViews.insight: The term translated as "conspiracy" in Judah indicates betrayal or perfidy, not just common disagreement; the rebellion against the Lord is treated as a rupture of covenant.
The people kept religious words and ceremonies, but their worship was insincere, because they did not love God or others.
The expression about the green oliver describes Judah as previously fertile and beautiful, but now delivered to the fire of judgment for having degenerated.

questions: In which areas can I be maintaining religious language, but resisting concrete obedience to God's voice?
What does the chapter teach about the difference between asking God for help and living in covenant with God?
How to react when fidelity to the Lord generates opposition even from close people?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to sincerity before God. Examine whether your devotion is accompanied by obedience, justice, and real repentance. When you notice hardness in your heart, confess it without excuses. And, like Jeremiah, give God the cause that you cannot defend alone, without answering evil with personal vengeance. A concrete application is to separate a time this week to identify an area in which you clearly know the will of God, but you are still delaying it, and take a practical attitude of obedience.
study.uncertainty: Some notes offer historical interpretations and hypotheses, such as the possible date in the reign of Zedekiah; this cannot be affirmed as certain only based on the text. Verse 15 contains difficult figurative language, and the notes understand it as a reference to insincere worship and the lack of love for God and others. References to Israel and Judah in the chapter can be read broadly in the notes, without allowing more detailed conclusions than they themselves offer.
